title: Blood Meridian
description: Epic historical novel by Cormac McCarthy
wiki_lead:
Blood Meridian or the Evening Redness in the West, commonly known as Blood Meridian, is a 1985 epic historical novel by American author Cormac McCarthy, classified as an anti-Western and Gothic Western. McCarthy's fifth book, it was published by Random House.
Set in the American frontier and drawing on historical events, the narrative follows a fictional teenager from Tennessee referred to as "the Kid", with the bulk of the text devoted to his experiences with the Glanton gang, a historical group of scalp hunters who massacred American Indians and others in the United States–Mexico borderlands from 1849 to 1850 for bounty, sadistic pleasure, and eventually, out of nihilistic habit. Judge Holden gradually emerges as the novel's antagonist, a physically massive, highly educated, preternaturally skilled member of the gang with pale and hairless skin who relishes the destruction and domination of whatever he encounters, including children and docile animals.
Although the novel initially received lukewarm critical and commercial reception, it has since become highly acclaimed and is widely recognized as McCarthy's magnum opus and one of the greatest American novels of all time, with some labelling the work as the Great American Novel.

Plot
The novel follows a young man who is never directly named, only being referred to as "the Kid." The Kid was born in Tennessee during the Leonid meteor shower of 1833. At 14, he runs away and travels across several states, arriving in Nacogdoches, Texas, where he enters a tent in which a reverend is giving a sermon. Judge Holden enters and announces that the reverend is a wanted imposter, detailing excessive crimes and inciting the crowd to violence. The Judge reveals shortly afterward that he had never met the reverend, and caused the lynching for no reason at all. The Kid escapes, encountering and brawling with a mercenary named Toadvine, but later assists him with arson and assault. The Kid sees the Judge as he escapes town, and the Judge smiles at him.
In Bexar, the Kid kills a bartender for refusing him a drink. He is persuaded to join Captain White's company of ill-equipped filibusters. The militia is overwhelmed by Comanche warriors. The Kid escapes and wanders about with Sproule, another survivor of the massacre. After walking through a village ravaged by Comanches, the two force their way onto a wagon and ride to a nearby town, Sproule dying along the way. Soldiers later seize the Kid and take him to jail in Chihuahua City, where he finds Toadvine. Toadvine arranges for the pair and another inmate to be released into a gang of scalphunters led by a former Texas Ranger and cavalry veteran named John Joel Glanton. The Judge is in company.

grok_lead: Blood Meridian, or the Evening Redness in the West is a novel by American author Cormac McCarthy, first published in 1985. The work chronicles the exploits of a teenage protagonist known only as "the kid," who in the 1840s and 1850s joins a band of scalp hunters led by the historical figure John Joel Glanton along the Texas-Mexico borderlands. Loosely drawn from real events, including the Glanton expedition's commission to eliminate Apache raiders before devolving into widespread atrocities against civilians and indigenous peoples, the narrative unfolds as a procession of unremitting carnage amid the harsh deserts of the American Southwest and northern Mexico. Central to the story is the towering, erudite antagonist Judge Holden, whose philosophical monologues on violence as an elemental force underpin the book's unflinching examination of human savagery, the ontology of war, and the illusory nobility of frontier expansion. Despite initial commercial underperformance and polarizing responses to its graphic depictions of brutality, Blood Meridian has achieved canonical status in American literature, frequently acclaimed as McCarthy's magnum opus and a profound revision of the Western genre that confronts the raw causality of conquest and depravity without moral equivocation.
